title: Georgia Merritt stages contemporary design show at London antiques dealer
description: Emerging designer Georgia Merritt has unveiled Refrain, an east London exhibition of sculptural furniture pieces informed by 18th-century architectural mouldings and musical staves. Refrain is the second solo show for Merritt , who was featured in our London Design Festival Dezeen Dispatch lineup of London's rising stars . Refrain is Georgia Merritt's second solo design show staged at antiques dealer M Kardana The exhibition brings together five of Merritt's pieces arranged across M Kardana , a 20th-century antiques shop on Hackney Road that was stripped back to form a gallery setting to accommodate the works. "My pieces can be read as furniture, but equally as sculptures, or propositions for an interior," Merritt told Dezeen. "Showing them at M Kardana, within the context of an antiques dealer, plays on that ambiguity." The exhibition includes a mirror that reveals Merritt's faux marble technique The design of each of Merritt's pieces was rooted in the inspiration she finds in the precision of both musical notation and architecture. Among them is a slim, wall-mounted mirror flanked by a duo of black lacquered doors that open out on full-length piano hinges. A floor lamp was topped with layers of organza Although made of birchwood, the doors look as if they are solid stone thanks to Merritt's distinctive painting technique, which involves hand-painting timber to create trompe l'œil faux marble furniture. The designer developed the granular process during a gilding apprenticeship that she completed when struggling to find work as a fine art graduate in 2020. Underscore is a wooden bench supported by a single leg Also on display is a delicate, hand-formed wire lamp encased in an ellipsoid shade made of silk organza overlaid with gazar. The lamp and its shade were positioned atop a stainless steel frame fitted with a central, rectilinear tray. Underscore is a sweeping bench supported by a single leg at one end, and resting against a wall at the other. The curved seating was carved from smooth sapele wood. Merritt wanted to visually interpret a glissando , the musical term for sliding from one note to the next. An low-slung table was topped with a textile canopy "The bench's profile recalls both Georgian architectural mouldings and the parallel lines of a musical stave," said the designer. A glass tablet was fitted atop the furniture's single leg, which was selected to echo a magnifying glass or other "apparatus for observation or examination". Merritt's fourth piece is a low-slung glass table, topped with an elongated canopy made of ivory silk that was clamped to the upper panes of glass with stainless-steel arms. Read: How London designers are making it work The final piece in the exhibition is another wall-mounted mirror fastened with piano hinges, but this one is full length and finished entirely in black lacquer. "When closed, the mirror's doors form a monolithic, modernist silhouette," said Merritt. Another all-black mirror features in the exhibition Refrain marks the second show that the designer has presented at M Kardana, following her Vague Precision exhibition in 2023. The designer considered how her practice, which she defines as art as much as design, has developed in recent years. "I think I'm continually working towards expressing something that I can sense quite clearly but can't necessarily define," she said. "With this exhibition, I feel a little closer to it." Merritt is interested in making pieces with an "ability to move between different contexts, whether that's a gallery, a domestic interior, or somewhere else". "I like the idea that their identity might shift slightly depending on where they're placed," she said. The designer was among the creatives showing in the Max Radford Gallery presentation at London's Collect fair in February. The photography is by Tazy Jessett Nash . Refrain is on display at M Kardana , 188A Hackney Road, London E2 7QL, United Kingdom, from 9 to 31 October 2026. title: Diana Kellogg updates her Tribeca home using salvaged materials
description: New York architect Diana Kellogg has renovated her historic Tribeca residence, highlighting materials repurposed from its industrial past. Kellogg and her family have occupied the home on Staple Street for 25 years, which is close to the studio that the architect shares with her filmmaker husband. Diana Kellogg has updated her home gradually over time, while retaining its industrial character The building originally served as cold storage for neighbouring produce distribution facilities, then became a plumber's supply storefront and eventually a residence around 50 years ago. Kellogg has renovated and updated the structure gradually over the years, and when her kids moved out, she decided to undertake a more comprehensive overhaul. Many of the built-in elements are formed from the salvage of the building's freight elevator An old freight elevator was removed and replaced with a space that Kellogg refers to as the Green Room. The glass-wrapped nook is lined with cushioned seating and used for intimate catch-ups over drinks, or private video calls. The kitchen similarly utilises salvaged elements The salvage from the elevator and other elements around the building were repurposed to create structures for the kitchen, bookcases, and a staircase that connects the four levels. "Throughout the house there were old glass and steel doors, and windows and stuff," Kellogg said. "I just moved them around and repurposed them." A space dubbed the Green Room is used for catch-ups and Zoom calls In keeping with the architecture, the decor remains industrial and spare, highlighting key elements like the fireplace and the 25-foot-long chestnut beams that span the ceiling. "It was a massive pain in the neck to strip those, but one of the best decisions we made, because they add so much warmth and character," said Kellogg. A steel staircase connects the home's four levels During the most recent renovation, the upstairs bedrooms with vaulted brick ceilings were reconfigured as neutrally decorated spaces separated by sliding mahogany doors. On the ground floor, the children's former playroom – complete with climbing ropes and a swing – was converted into a comfortable TV room, featuring a large L-shaped sofa and a variety of midcentury furniture pieces. The ground-floor children's playroom was recently converted into a media room Matching those on the level above, Noguchi pendant lights hang from the steel beams that Kellogg added to suspend the "jungle gym". "There's still one climbing rope down there that people think is an art piece, which I love," she said. Read: Crina Arghirescu Rogard adds "eccentric design" to historic penthouse in Tribeca Key artworks include a pair of photographs by Ljubodrag Andric , which he produced to sit either side of the first-floor fireplace and "give the place so much depth and warmth," said Kellogg. Downstairs, the walls are adorned with images of The Rajkumari Ratnavati Girl's School that Kellogg completed in 2021 in India's Thar Desert. Upstairs bedrooms are divided by mahogany sliding doors The roof terrace was relandscaped with planters and a variety of wooden outdoor furniture that forms dining and seating areas with views of a historic bridge between the adjacent buildings. "I really wanted an oasis up there, and to have it be a second living room," said Kellogg. "And there's the fabulous bridge, which we have kind of great views of from our house – which is, in my opinion, better than actually being inside it." The roof terrace was also refurbished with planters and outdoor furniture Many of Tribeca's former industrial buildings are now residential, housing large lofts and penthouses, while others contain galleries and creative spaces. Examples of other homes in the neighbourhood include a penthouse in the American Thread Building updated by Crina Arghirescu Rogard and a loft that Andrea Leung renovated to conceal "secret spaces". title: The two forces that help build opportunity
description: Hey pals, I hope all is good in your world. Today we are going to dive a little deeper into two very important elements that build recognisable reputations and brands… and why I built the Opportunity Design Course + Course Club (Early Bird enrollment closes this Sunday!). The two elements? Perception & Evidence. Firstly I want to explain what these two things are individually. Evidence: This is what you’ve actually done. It’s the real, tangible proof of your work. The products you’ve built, the testimonials you’ve earned from your clients, the projects you’ve delivered to your people, the impact you’ve created as a whole. It’s the truth, the receipts, the stuff that stands up in a court of freaking law. Perception: This is what people think you’ve done. It’s how your brand is experienced from the outside. It’s the story that forms in someone’s head long before they ever meet you, talk to you, or work with you. Simply put... Evidence = what is true and provable. Perception = what people believe to be true based on what they can see. The big old problem we all have as creative humans, especially those who have been in the game for a fair chunk of time... it’s impossible for anyone to have access to ALL of your evidence. Most people won’t see the hours you’ve poured in a project, the thinking behind your decisions, or how much bloody effort goes into what you do every damn day. They often just see the end result and that’s where their opinion forms. That’s why perception, in many cases, outweighs evidence... and why perception is super important in brand building. You could be absolutely brilliant at what you do, but if nobody knows it, it doesn’t exist in their world. You might have the work to back it up, but if the way you show up looks sloppy or inconsistent... or you do not show up at all... people will think twice and find another option. That doesn’t mean perception is about pretending or faking it for the internet or your clients in general. It’s about making it easier for people to find the truth, and to do that, you need to give them access to your evidence. Our job as humans who own businesses is to make sure the perception of us from the outside aligns with the truth as closely as possible. Trust doesn’t come from either perception or evidence on its own… it grows when the two work together, and as you can see from the image below, that’s when you become a Power Brand. I personally believe we are all striving to become the “Power Brand” where our perception and evidence are high and in alignment, and the gap between them is very small. This is where true value is created and we become a much safer commercial choice for our clients. Opportunity happens consistently when the truth and perceived reality are best mates, standing together. Here is a little breakdown of each quadrant so you can understand where you might sit. High perception, high evidence: The Power Brand. People notice you and consistently experience the quality behind the perception. Your reputation matches the reality of what you actually deliver, which creates trust, momentum, and long-term opportunity. Every great brand we know masters this balance between perception and evidence. High perception, low evidence: The Hype Brand. You know how to grab attention and create excitement, but the reality underneath hasn’t fully caught up yet. Things can look bigger, stronger, or more established from the outside than they actually are once people get closer. Low perception, high evidence: The Hidden Genius Brand. You’re doing brilliant work, but not enough people currently get the chance to experience it. The skill, care, and trustworthiness are already there… your reputation just hasn’t spread far beyond your existing network yet. (I built Opportunity Design for you my friends) Low perception, low evidence: The Work-in-Progress Brand. You’re still figuring things out, experimenting, learning, and discovering where your strengths actually live. And honestly? That’s completely normal. Every powerful brand, business, and creative human starts as a work in progress. The big takeaway here? Branding isn’t just about reality... it’s also about perceived reality. People can’t choose you based on the evidence they have never seen. They can only choose you based on what they know, and ultimately, believe to be true about you. This is a 6-week programme designed to help you close the gap between what you’re capable of and what other people know you’re capable of, in order to create more extraordinary opportunities. title: The Industry Swap Experiment
description: An amazingly random thing happened this last week. I found myself in Moab, Utah, with around 70 total strangers who now feel like my best friends. I was invited by my buddy Jason to speak at the first-ever Summer Camp hosted by his company, Rupt, for the promotional products industry. There were team colours, a healthy dose of friendly competition, prizes, adventures and learning sessions, all set against the incredible backdrop of the Colorado River and the red rock desert. It was fucking Magical. As a brand guy I often find myself around brand people whether thats agency owners, designers or people building things in the creative space but I have always loved to pop myself in the deep water of the unknowing. I know very little about this world. Like most people, I’ve interacted with the industry countless times as an end user. Whether that’s branded merch, company swag, event giveaways or promotional products arriving in the post… but I’ve never actually spent too much time inside the industry itself or with the people who make it all happen… so on paper, I had absolutely no business being there. But that’s exactly why I jumped at the chance to speak at this event. I love learning new things, and this room was packed with some of the biggest hitters in the game. People who have spent years building businesses and solving problems in a world I know jack shit about. It would have been easy to say no. The travel was long, the industry was unfamiliar but saying no to this opportunity was never really on the cards for me. I am getting older, and as that happens, the more I think one of the biggest mistakes we make is only learning from people who do the same thing as us. We all read the same design books, follow pretty much the same people, attend the same conferences and end up having the same conversations over and over again. This felt like the exact opposite of that… I’m gonna call it the ‘anti-echo chamber’ move. An opportunity to step outside my own little corner of the world and spend time with people who think differently and see things through a completely different lens. I had a feeling it would open my brain up in ways it hadn’t been before, and it absolutely did. Now, even though this space doesn’t live and breathe design in the same way mine does, it still lives in the world of branding. Most brand people spend their time on the fun stuff like the thinking, story, and execution side of design. We help make strategic decisions, build the identity, and create the funky punky assets. Then, more often than not, we release the work into the wild and hope it finds its way. What really hit home for me whilst spending time with this incredible group of humans is that this industry is actually much closer to mine than I first realised. They’re positioned at an incredibly important point in the journey… where the identity of a company meets real humans in the real world. They are a key part of what we do because they help bring businesses to life through experiences. And ultimately, that’s where ‘brand status’ is earned. As brand people, we’re in the game of pattern building and memory. We help businesses become recognisable. The promotional products industry helps those companies show up in the real world, creating physical touch-points and experiences that reinforce everything the business is trying to stand for. The biggest takeaway for me this week, apart from the fact that Moab might be one of the coolest places on the planet, is that every industry has its own wisdom. Every industry has people solving interesting problems and has a lot of knowledge to offer the general outsider who is keen to learn a new perspective. It’s easy to convince ourselves that all the answers live inside our own little bubble, but I’ve found over the years that many of the best ideas and implementations in my own business have come from looking outside of design. Whether that’s borrowing hospitality thinking and applying it to my design process, or building an identity of my own that fuses tattoo culture with skate-shop vibes, the things that have helped me stand out have not come from simply doing what everyone else was doing. One of the ideas I shared during my talk was Hotelling’s Law … the observation that competitors naturally drift towards sameness because it feels safer. Over time, everyone starts looking similar, sounding similar and offering similar things because nobody wants to stray too far from what appears to be working for others. The irony though is that the safest thing to do often becomes the riskiest thing to do. If everybody moves towards the middle, the middle becomes really freaking crowded. Which is why I’ve always been more interested in pushing at the edges… That’s where the interesting opportunities live. That’s why I think we should all spend a little more time making anti-echo chamber moves. Here are some ways you can do that: 1. Go to the event that isn’t built for you. 2. Read the book that nobody in your industry is talking about. 3. Spend time with people who challenge your assumptions. 4. Put yourself in rooms where you’re not the expert. Remember, my friends… curiosity is often where the magic lives. And if my week in the Utah desert taught me anything, it’s that sometimes the most valuable thing you can do isn’t go deeper into your own world… It’s to spend some time exploring somebody else’s. Big love and respect. James - The People’s Branding Mentor

title: Tiny moments that become a real brand.
description: Before we jump into this week’s article, reminder that my new book No Bullsh*t Branding is available for pre-order… and if you pre-order by the end of today (Sunday 31st May) you get a bonus freebie bundle, including the Book Club, the new MVB Course, limited edition MBJ merch, and digital downloads. Check it out here ! Thank you all so much for your support. Last weekend the weather was delicious. So delicious that myself, Kate and Rocco went to the beach for the day to hang with our friends (Jamie & Mel) and their little kiddos… it was one of those beautiful little days that will live long in the memory bank. We were down at West Wittering beach near Chichester. It’s this big, magical stretch of sand where, when the tide goes out, the beach becomes absolutely colossal. Perfect for kids because there’s endless space to run around and play… it becomes the worlds largest, sandy adventure space. Scattered across the beach are these little pools of warm water left behind by the retreating tide… tiny, stinky lakes full of seaweed, shells, wet sand and mess. Basically heaven for a little dude like Rocco. And he was more than happy exploring them completely alone while the rest of his friends sat further up the beach eating lunch and digging holes. He was so happy, so I wanted him to just ‘be’… so I stayed and watched. After maybe an hour of watching him play in the same giant puddle, I eventually wandered up to him and asked him to come back to “base camp” so we could put more suncream on, tag mummy back in and potentially allow me to eat some lunch. But he was having absolutely none of it. Everything I offered was ignored. Every negotiation tactic I’d learned in business was useless, and every attempt to reason with him about how the sun was really hot and he needed protecting from it was completely pointless. Eventually Kate, my wonderful wife, spotted my slow descent into parental defeat from afar and wandered over with all the supplies we needed. And at that point, I just accepted reality and decided to play the waiting game until he was ready to move on himself… I mean, the sun would go down eventually, I was sure of that, and I also now had a sandwich. But there was a lesson hiding inside all of this. When you have very little to negotiate with, the situation you are in becomes incredibly difficult to win… and this got me thinking about the very beginning of my own business journey. It was so difficult to find any money-making opportunities when I started because I had so little to negotiate with. No Leverage. I had no real portfolio, no website, no testimonials and, in absolute honesty… very little knowledge. I wouldn’t have hired me. As you know, for me, a brand is a recognisable reputation, and at that point I was neither recognised nor did I really have a reputation worth knowing… unless it was “having a good time down the pub” - I was real good at that. And this got me thinking about all the newbies entering the world right now. All the junior creatives trying to find work and carve out a place for themselves while also navigating challenges I never had to deal with. Things like social media pressure, constant comparison, AI, tech and the heavy, heavy, heavy psychological weight of feeling like you need to live your life so publicly online. Now, I’m not saying my era had it easy at all… every generation has its own struggles. But I do think it’s harder now than it was 20 years ago, mainly for the reasons I mentioned above. So I want to try an answer this question today. How do we build a business when, right at the beginning, we have nothing to be recognised for and no reputation backing us up? So… lets chat. Yes, you might not have the clients yet. You might not have the case studies, the swanky portfolio, the testimonials or the years of industry proof backing up your ambition. But what you do have is YOU. That matters far more than many people think. Because there are already so many things you are recognised for outside of your “business circles”. Your attitude, your energy, your humour, your kindness, your curiosity, your willingness to help, your ability to make people feel good around you, your ability to stay optimistic when everything feels difficult or half empty. What I’m trying to suggest here is that even if you do not yet have a recognisable reputation around your work, you already have years and years of building a recognisable reputation around your humanness and character, and that is a beautifully fun place to start… that becomes your negotiating power. One of the huge advantages early stage creatives have is that they are not yet boxed in by the “rules” of the industry. They are not trapped by client expectations or weighed down by years of process refinement and predictability. They still have “all the raws”… raw energy, raw enthusiasm and raw creativity to boot. In the beginning, it’s often your willingness to care about others and build relationships that sparks the most opportunity. Helping a mate out for freebies, offering your services to friends of friends in exchange for tickets to their latest gig… that scrappy little world of free crafty goodness is where most of us cut our teeth in the industry. When I was starting out, I bartered constantly. I used my skills to build experience, and the more experience I gained, the more confidence I built. In return, I’d get free coffee, free jewellery, free food, whilst also building relationships with local humans… whatever people could offer at the time instead of money, I said yes to. Looking back, I actually think there’s something incredibly beautiful about that stage of the journey. I mean, bartering is how worlds were built. When you’re starting out, you still have permission to try almost anything you can to keep the lights on and keep the dream alive. You can knock on doors, start conversations, help people, make things, experiment, build fabulous little ditties and push your creativity out into the world. And over time, people begin recognising you for those behaviours. For your energy, your effort, your generosity, your consistency and the way you make people feel. Almost without noticing it, those tiny moments become the foundations of a recognisable reputation. A real brand. So if you are at the beginning, listening to a noisy world telling you that “designers are fucked” or “the creative industry is doomed,” remember that most of it is just distraction… like a lot of news on the inter webs. Don’t fall into the trap of blindly listening to these people. Many of them have their own agenda too… which is often making sure they stay relevant and irreplaceable in a changing world. Instead, use your creativity and your energy to build relationships. Make cool stuff and send it to people. Write a little hand-drawn note thanking somebody for inspiring you. Instead of sending the same PDF portfolio to 400 people like everybody else is doing, start more real, human conversations. Barter your services. Collaborate with people. Send a hand written letter. Deliver someone a little product with your work on it. Go above and beyond simply because you care enough to do so. Become recognised for how much effort you are putting in… that is a reputation that opportunities will eventually flow towards. Stay Focused, Stay Crafty… Your creativity is your super duper power. James - The Peoples Branding Mentor

title: The Unscriptable Moments That Build Reputation
description: Hello my champions of creative goodness. How are ya? Today I want to dive into a little topic that I am super passionate about, and that is the human goodness we can do to elevate the experience for the people we work with. Everyone reading this is a craft-based, creativity-infused builder of things. You might own a business, work with brands, or create cool visuals for people who love looking at cool visuals. I don’t think creative people like that need motivation to continue doing the things they already do so well, but I do think there is another layer we often forget to think about… the human layer. The stuff on top of the craft. That is where some new magic can be found. It looks like over the coming years a lot of businesses and brands will automate huge parts of their customer journey, which is logical, so the question for me becomes… Where does the human come in and make a decision that was not obvious? I am all for becoming more efficient and dialling in a good process, as many of you will know, but it’s often the stupid-on-paper, “not good for business” decisions that build a reputation worth talking about. One of my favourite examples of human creativity elevating a brand’s reputation is the story of Joshie the Giraffe. A family went on holiday to California and accidentally left their son’s stuffed giraffe at a Ritz-Carlton hotel where they were staying. To put the little boy at ease, his dad told a little white lie and said Joshie had decided to stay behind for an extra holiday. The dad had phoned the hotel and asked if they could find it, send it back, and hopefully reunite the little guy with his giraffe. The hotel staff found Joshie amongst the laundry and could have simply posted the toy back. But instead, they created an entire photo album showing Joshie relaxing by the pool, driving golf carts, getting spa treatments with cucumbers over his eyes, and “enjoying his extended vacation” before finally sending him home, all to back up his dad’s story. That tiny, unscriptable moment of human creativity transformed a forgotten toy into a story that millions of people still talk about today… just like I am right now. And I think that’s freaking fascinating. Because I doubt that family remembers much about the facilities at the Ritz-Carlton, the weather, or even how good the food was… but they will absolutely remember Joshie’s holiday forever. This got the old curiosity up… Why do moments like this stick with us so deeply while so many other experiences disappear from memory almost immediately? Why do we instantly want to tell our mates about them, repost them online and emotionally connect with complete strangers because of them? For that we probably need to get a little ‘sciencey’. Now remember, I’m not a scientist. I’m just an inquisitive bloke with a scraggly beard who spends far too much time researching human behaviour, but here’s what I found out… Your brain is basically a very clever prediction machine. Most of the time, your brain is trying to conserve energy by guessing what is about to happen next based on previous experiences and familiar patterns. If things go exactly as expected, the brain doesn’t need to pay much attention because nothing new or important is happening. Win for brain power. This is why most of our routine experiences disappear from memory almost immediately. If you are anything like me, you get in the car, drive somewhere you’ve been a thousand times before, pull up, get out, and suddenly realise you barely even remember the journey itself. You obviously drove, stopped at traffic lights and avoided crashing into things, but because your brain already knew the pattern, most of the drive happened on complete autopilot… and it’s even easier now I don’t have to change gears anymore. Thank fook for the automatic. Humans do this constantly. We predict things, filter things and automate familiar experiences because if we had to consciously process every tiny detail of every moment of every day we would mentally collapse before our cheeky 11am coffee break. That’s why so many experiences we go through every single day become, well… forgettable. You expect the hotel room to be ready when you arrive. You expect somebody at reception to hand you a key, point you towards the lift or stairs and solve any mini problems in the quickest and most logical way possible, so when all of those things happen exactly as predicted, your brain simply processes the experience efficiently and moves on because nothing emotionally interesting actually happened. But when something interrupts that predictable pattern in a creative, emotional or unexpected way, your brain suddenly pays far more attention because it wasn’t expecting it. That’s why the Joshie story mattered so freaking much. The family expected the hotel to find the giraffe and simply post it back. Problem solved. No dramas here people. Everybody moves on with their lives. But instead, the hotel staff created this ridiculously brilliant, fake holiday for the giraffe that made it feel like Joshie was genuinely out there living his best life in the California sun and making mates along the way. They went to completely unreasonable measures just to bring a little bit of joy to a child and back up his dad’s white lie, and that exact unpredictability is what made the whole thing unforgettable. Humans remember meaningful and surprising moments far more than they remember predictable and functional ones. The hotel didn’t just solve the problem. They transformed a completely ordinary customer service interaction into a story that people are still retelling years later… and I think that’s the bit most of us miss as business owners. People rarely remember what was efficient, but they almost always remember how something made them feel. I mean, I almost bloody cried the first time I read the Joshie story because I instantly thought about how my own son would feel seeing his favourite toy off living its best life and making mates on holiday. I take Lightning McQueen with me on work trips because I miss my son Rocco, and I take silly little photos of him at random places because I know my son lights up when he sees them. He genuinely thinks daddy and Lightning are away together having a good time, so this little giraffe story hit a proper emotional note for me. The Joshie story stopped being “good customer service” and instantly became something far more human because you could feel the love, effort and humanity inside the decision those hotel staff made… and that kind of creativity can never be automated. Nor bloody should it. I hope this story sparks the creativity inside you to go against the grain when you can. To be unpredictable with your kindness and to find ways to connect with others that might be out of the ordinary. People remember people who thought about them in different and unique ways. I think, over the coming years, businesses and brands will increasingly be judged on what they choose to keep human. Automate the predictable. Humanise the meaningful. Love ya. James - The People’s Branding Mentor

title: The Personal Brand Trap: Why Humans Shouldn’t Think of Themselves as Brands
description: When I was a wee little boy growing up, I wanted to be a fireman. It seemed considerably more achievable than becoming a ThunderCat or Batman, which were my other career choices when I was eight. At school I had absolutely no clue what I wanted to do as a career. Potentially something arty or sporty, but back in the 90s I was told neither of those were money-makers, so I had to think about getting a proper job. Today, I would classify myself as a designer and educator helping the next generation of creatives build more opportunity for themselves. That feels very aligned with who I am today. But I have also been a barman, factory worker, waiter, tattoo apprentice, window cleaner, failed businessman, unemployable bum, and many other things on the journey to finding this particular version of me. And that is one of the wonderful things about being a human… nobody really freaking knows who they’re going to become. The person you are today is probably very different from the person you were five years ago, and if you’re doing this thing called life properly, there’s a good chance the person you’ll become five years from now will look different again. And, from what my mum tells me… that’s completely normal. Most of us are making it up as we go, collecting experiences and continuously falling forward into newer versions of ourselves… we’re supposed to evolve. So in this little article I want to share my perspective on a topic that I think deserves a little more questioning: personal branding. More specifically, I want to explore why I don’t think humans should think of themselves as brands, and why applying brand logic to a human being can potentially do more harm than good. Thanks for reading The Real Brand Life! Subscribe for free to receive new posts. Now, I’m not here to suggest that personal branding doesn’t exist. That would cause a riot. Instead, I’d like to challenge some of the advice being peddled around willy-nilly on the dopamine drug train that is social media. To do that, I think we first need to agree on the difference between brand logic and human logic. A brand’s job is to reduce complexity. Brands are trying to be recognised at scale and for that to happen, they need to simplify things. They need to make themselves easier to understand, remember and choose. They do that better when they are associated with a couple of very clear ideas. Humans, on the other hand, operate very differently my friends. We change our minds all the freaking time. We become interested in new things. We learn stuff, we grow our minds and then we see the world differently because of it. And an important thing to add is that humans don’t naturally operate at scale. We evolved in small communities and tribes, not in front of thousands of random people online. So if brands become stronger through consistency and humans become stronger through change, are we really sure those two things belong together? That’s why I find phrases like “you are your brand” and “everyone has a personal brand” a little, well… problematic. Being known for something and being a brand are not the same thing. I understand that these phrases are often being used as shortcuts, but even when I account for that nuance, I still think they fundamentally misunderstand what a brand is… and what a human needs. Now, I don’t want this to come across as a rant or a black-and-white argument, as some of the advice coming out of the personal brand camp is incredibly useful. Visibility matters for sure because if nobody knows what the heck you do, how on earth are they supposed to hire you? Other people need to know you exist people. I absolutely believe humans should become known. Known for doing good work, having interesting ideas, standing for something and making a positive impact on the people around them. But becoming known and becoming a product are not the same thing. Being known, or what most would simply call a reputation, is something people gift you over time. It forms through your behaviour and the way you consistently show up for yourself. You don’t have to manufacture it, force it or spend every waking minute trying to manage how you’re perceived by others. A reputation happens naturally as you continue growing into the person you’re becoming. And this is where I think we can run into trouble because the moment we start thinking of ourselves as a brand, our focus can shift. Instead of asking, “Who am I becoming?” we start asking, “How will this look to other people?” The danger is that we start viewing ourselves through the eyes of an audience before we’ve had chance to fully understand ourselves… we start looking at ourselves from the outside in. At first, that might not sound like too much of a problem. In fact, it actually sounds pretty bloody sensible. If you’re running a business, surely you should care about how people feel when they see you. But I don’t believe growth and perception always want the same thing. The thing about growth is that it can look a bit messy from the outside. You change your mind, let go of old ideas and, more often than we’d like to admit, realise you got something wrong. That’s all part of the process. And brand logic doesn’t particularly reward that kind of thinking. Brands gain strength through their consistency. They keep showing up in roughly the same way until people know exactly what to expect from them. And I think that’s where a lot of people can run into a bit of an issue. The more successful a personal brand becomes, the more pressure there can be to keep being the person your audience already knows. To keep talking about the same things, showing up in the same way and feeding the machine that made people pay attention in the first place. That’s the personal brand trap. The human becomes responsible for holding onto a version of themselves they may have already outgrown. And as we see more people choosing freelance careers, building solo businesses and creating opportunities for themselves online, I think this becomes an increasingly important conversation to navigate. I know that perception matters, visibility matters, being known matters, and creating opportunity matters… but so does growth as a human being. Perhaps the challenge isn’t figuring out how to turn people into brands… instead it’s figuring out how to help people become known without trapping them. I’d hate to think that personal branding, the very thing so many people turn to in search of more opportunity, could end up becoming the thing that stops them from becoming who they’re supposed to be. So if I can leave you with a little bit of advice here it would be this: focus on the things you want to be known for, but don’t lose sight of the person you’re becoming along the way. Maybe the goal isn’t to manage perception at all. Perhaps it’s simply to become someone worth paying attention to. Humans are supposed to evolve. Brands are supposed to repeat. The problems arise when we start applying the rules of one to the other, so don’t flatten yourself into a product mindset just because the internet tells you that’s the secret to success. Focus on becoming known for your craft, your kindness and your character. Keep sharing what matters to you because opportunity has a funny way of finding people who do. Just please remember to sprinkle a little patience on yourself along the way. Your mate, James Thoughts on this? Comment below team. I’m excited to hear what you think. title: Historic town hall in Limoges set on fire during French protests
description: Significant parts of the 143-year-old Limoges Town Hall in France have been destroyed in an arson attack, as protests broke out across the country over the weekend. On 17th October, Limoges Town Hall was set on fire. Videos taken by people on the ground show its slate roofs ablaze and its central bell tower collapsing. Officials have not yet confirmed the state of the town hall and whether the rest of the building is at risk of collapse, according to the BBC . Designed by French architect Charles-Alfred Leclerc, the neo-Renaissance Limoges Town Hall was built in 1883 and was listed as a historical monument in 1975. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Sky News (@skynews) The neo-Renaissance Limoges Town Hall has been damaged in a fire An estimated 550,000 people in France took to the streets over the weekend to protest the rising cost of living and poor school conditions. Some demonstrations turned to violence and disorder, with hundreds of shops being looted and destroyed. Around 2,400 people have been arrested . Read: Huge fire breaks out at Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris In addition to Limoges Town Hall, other buildings in France were set on fire in arson attacks, including a tourist office in Lyon . The mayor of Limoges has demanded a "Notre-Dame plan" to restore the town hall. A huge fire broke out at the iconic Notre-Dame Cathedral in Paris in 2019, which saw the Gothic landmark's 90-metre-high spire and parts of the roof collapse. After five years of reconstruction work, the cathedral reopened in 2024 with restored interiors and the spire rebuilt as a replica of the 1859 version lost to the fire. title: Karimoku New Standard and ASICS create furniture made from crushed trainers
description: Furniture brand Karimoku New Standard has announced the global release of its KNS x ASICS Collaboration, which repurposes upcycled foam from unused ASICS trainers as cushioning for two seating designs. The KNS x ASICS Collaboration uses deadstock and sample footwear from ASICS that would have otherwise been discarded. Karimoku New Standard, a sub-brand of Japanese manufacturer Karimoku , used the same technique that ASICS has utilised for its upcycled Neocurve trainers to create the material for the collaboration. ASICS trainers are crushed to extract EVA foam The ASICS footwear is dismantled, sorted and crushed to extract Ethylene Vinyl Acetate (EVA) foam, a flexible, light material commonly used as cushioning for midsoles, outsoles and footbeds. After the foam has been extracted, it is blended with cotton and paired with a three-millimetre condensed foam sheet to create a hybrid structure, according to Karimoku New Standard . The material is then used as cushioning in the brand's Castor Lobby Sofa and Polar Lounge Chair, which also feature an embroidered tag as a symbol of the collaboration. Read: Issey Miyake designs "minimalist" Hyper Taping trainers for ASICS The KNS x ASICS Collaboration, which was introduced in Japan earlier this year before the recent global launch, came about after Karimoku New Standard was working on seating for the meeting spaces in ASICS' Tokyo office. "Through rigorous sessions with ASICS – leveraging their expertise in sports science – and a meticulous adjustment process for real-world office use, Karimoku repeatedly prototyped to transform an unfamiliar material like shoe waste into true furniture comfort," Karimoku New Standard said. "This uncompromising, hands-on exploration led to the creation of the innovative hybrid structure," the brand continued. "Beyond merely reusing materials from a sustainability standpoint, it turns them into a functional added value." The Polar Lounge Chair was made using upcycled sneakers Karimoku has previously collaborated with brands including Zaha Hadid Design . ASICS recently released the "minimalist" Hyper Taping trainers with fashion brand Issey Miyake and has also designed pastel-coloured trainers with Danish brand Hay . title: What is "the gravity of average" and why is it holding you back?
description: I grew up believing one thing: Don’t be average. Looking back now, as an older, slightly fatter man, there’s something wonderfully ironic about that particular piece of advice. While every person in authority was telling me not to become average, the systems around me were teaching me exactly how to become it. School teaches us there was one right answer. Business teaches us there’s a right process. Algorithms tell us there’s a right format. Most industries have their own best practices, and society at large constantly reminds us that fitting in is safer than standing out. None of these proven systems are bad. In fact, they’re incredibly useful. They help us educate millions of little people, build reliable businesses, and make sense of an increasingly complicated world. But when you start stacking them on top of one another, year after year, decade after decade… something intriguing happens. They all pull us in the exact same direction: Toward what’s proven Toward what’s predictable Toward what’s familiar Toward the flipping middle We hear a lot these days about falling test scores, declining creativity, and a lack of ambition. I’m not convinced that’s the whole story. I think we’re living inside an ecosystem of invisible forces that constantly reward the safest path. Millions of perfectly sensible decisions, made by perfectly sensible people, combine to suck us toward the same ideas until we all end up in the exact same place… the fookin’ middle. I call this: the gravity of average. Whether we realize it or not, we’ve been caught in its invisible pull since the day we were born… damn it. Here are the five layers of gravity conspiring against us all, and why you need to fight them with everything you’ve got to protect your individual magic. 1. Educational gravity Our first experience of this gravity starts in the classroom. School has an incredibly difficult job: educating millions of children fairly and consistently, often with limited resources and enormous expectations. The only way to make that possible is to rely on standardized curricula, rigid grading schemes, and easily measured outcomes. From a very young age, we learn to optimize for what gets rewarded … the gold stars, the praise from teachers, the good-old pats on the back. Before long, we’re no longer just learning the subject, we’re learning how to succeed within the system. The educational environment doesn’t intentionally produce average people. Far from it. But when success is measured in the exact same way for everyone, it’s only natural that millions of children begin chasing the exact same things. The more people optimize for the identical outcome, the more they will eventually look alike… it’s the logical outcome of a predictable system. 2. Economic gravity Businesses only exist if they survive, and to do that, they have to make rational decisions. If a pricing model has worked before, why change it? If a marketing strategy has proven successful, why reinvent it? If a competitor is growing using a particular approach, it’s only natural to copy it. None of these are bad decisions. Economist Harold Hotelling described this exact phenomenon in what became known as Hotelling’s Law . When businesses compete for the same customers, they naturally drift toward one another rather than away. Differentiation feels risky, while similarity feels sensible. Over time, this way of thinking compounds. What starts as “best practice” gradually becomes the default way of doing business. When an entire industry chases the identical measures of success (revenue, profit, or market share), even the most original business ideas eventually drift toward the average when they optimize for the same thing. 3. Social gravity As humans, we’ve always worried about belonging. For most of human history, being accepted by the group dramatically increased our chances of not becoming dead. That instinct is still hardwired into us. One of my favourite psychology experiments that backs this up comes from Solomon Asch . Participants were invited into a room to complete what they thought was a simple test about the length of a few lines. What they didn’t know was that everyone else in the room was an actor hired to be in on the experiment. The answers were obvious, but one by one, the actors deliberately gave the wrong answer. Faced with an entire room disagreeing with them, many participants ignored what they could clearly see and went along with the crowd instead. Around 75% of people conformed at least once, even though the group was clearly wrong. Nobody has to tell us to fit in. We just learn which parts of ourselves earn acceptance and which parts are safer left hidden. 4. Algorithmic gravity Welcome to the newest kid on the block. Algorithms don’t care about “silly” things like originality… all they give a poop about is retention. The easiest way to predict what will keep your attention is to look at what has already worked. Successful ideas become recommendations. Recommendations become trends. Trends become the templates that every influencer and their dog starts copying. Before long, thousands of people are creating different versions of the exact same thing because that’s what the system keeps serving up. Social media isn’t in the business of finding the next brilliant idea. It’s in the business of keeping us scrolling, and scrolling, and scrolling. And the easiest way to do that is by feeding us a slightly repackaged version of the average… the baseline of everything the system has already gobbled up before. 5. Professional gravity Every profession develops its own “playbook.” Designers have processes, marketers have foolproof plans, and consultants have their frameworks. Most of these defaults exist because someone, at some point, solved a real problem for a real person… hurrah. The danger happens when best practice subtly becomes the only practice. The longer an approach survives unquestioned, the more it feels like common sense. Before long, entire industries are repeating formulas that worked 30 years ago, even though the world has completely evolved around them. The comfort zone is a very dangerous place. Nothing grows there, as they say. The optimization trap What I’ve realized about these five forces is that they all share the exact same mischievous mechanism. Every system must decide what success looks like and, once it does, the rest of us naturally optimize for it. School rewards grades. Business rewards revenue. Algorithms reward engagement. Society rewards acceptance. Professions reward best practice. None of the above are bad… but when millions of people chase the exact same measures of success, gravity takes over. Human beings are remarkably good at adapting to their environment. The more we align ourselves with the same definition of success, the more we begin to resemble one another. And today, more people than ever are finding themselves in the middle. For most of history, becoming competent at something took years of deliberate practice. Today, technology can get almost anyone to “good enough” in a matter of minutes. Technology is closing the gap from below, while optimization is closing the gap from above. People who once struggled to produce competent work can now create something perfectly passable with better tools. At the same time, many of the people who were once exceptional are handing more of their thinking over to those same tools. In the pursuit of speed they often sacrifice the originality and personality that made them stand out in the first place. One force lifts people into the middle. The other pulls people back towards it. Now, there is absolutely nothing wrong with being average. Millions of people build fulfilling careers, do meaningful work, and live brilliant lives without ever trying to stand out. But commercially, today, average is becoming a far riskier place to build a future. To riff on something Rory Sutherland once said: when you become logical, you become predictable. And when you become predictable, you become replaceable. That doesn’t mean you should reject logic or stop using new technology. It simply means those things are no longer enough. They help you meet the standard, yes, but they’ll never make you the obvious choice. I’ve come to believe that opportunity doesn’t flow toward the middle. It flows toward recognizable differences that people trust. The gravity of average never disappears. You simply decide whether to drift with it… or spend your time pushing against it. Maybe that’s what Mr. Hotelling was trying to tell us all along. Test the edges. - James This article first appeared in my Fast Company column. You can check it out here .

title: Golf clubhouse by Graham Baba nods to farm structures in rural Washington
description: US studio Graham Baba Architects used timber and board-formed concrete to create "warmth and depth" at the Westwood Golf clubhouse and driving range in an agricultural region. The project completed a refresh of the nine-hole golf course in the central Washington town of Yakima. Graham Baba Architects has completed a golf clubhouse in Washington The semi-arid region is known for its orchards and hop fields, which the architects drew upon while conceiving the clubhouse and driving range. "The new facilities are designed as a minimalist nod to agrarian structures," said Graham Baba Architects , a Seattle studio. The building is a "minimalist nod" to agrarian structures The star element is the newly constructed, 12,000-square-foot (1,115-square-metre) clubhouse, which rises two levels and is L-shaped in plan. It contains hospitality space and 28 driving-range stations, including high-tech ones that can simulate golf courses found across the world. Mass timber was used for the structure The roof and upper floor are made of mass timber panels, supported by steel and glued-laminated columns and beams. There is a 20-foot (6-metre) clear span between columns, allowing for unencumbered golf swings. Shade screens made of Corten-steel wrap certain areas of the building The facility departs from the standard driving-range facility in terms of its materiality. "In contrast to more typical pan-deck and painted concrete driving ranges, the exposed timber structure introduces warmth and depth, creating a space that is as much about experience as it is about performance," the team said. The ground level contains a restaurant Shade screens made of Corten steel wrap select areas of the building. Wooden boards were used to form the concrete walls, helping soften the building's expression. "The texture breaks down the scale of the concrete and introduces a horizontal rhythm that reinforces the building's low profile across the flat site," the team said. "As light rakes across the surface, the lines draw the eye toward framed views of the green beyond." Read: "World's first" self-driving golf trolley follows players around the course The ground level holds a restaurant , bar and pro shop, along with 14 driving range bays. The upper floor houses 14 additional bays, a second bar and an enclosed event space. A broad terrace overlooks the golf course. "The lower range is more protected and shaded, shielded from wind and direct sun," the team said. 28 driving ranges are spread between its two levels "The upper level opens more fully to the air, capturing cross breezes and long views in both directions." Below the building is a golf cart garage and a supplemental kitchen to support the restaurant. The site also includes a green roof and an on-site stormwater management system, which channels rainwater to a pond. The water is used to irrigate the site during the summer months. Other golf facilities include an indoor club in Montreal by Ivy Studio that features rich shades of green and burgundy, and a golf performance centre in Los Angeles by HA+MA that is made of Alaskan cedar and handmade Danish bricks. The photography is by Kevin Scott . title: NM3 designs "truly classic bar for Milan"
description: Local studio NM3 looked to Vienna's iconic 20th-century American Bar by Adolf Loos when designing the bespoke red-hued interior of Milan's Bar Bardo. When designing the project, NM3 drew on the influential design of Loos's famous bar , an early modernist landmark finished in 1908. Bar Bardo was designed by NM3 "The American Bar was more of an aspiration than a direct formal reference," studio co-founder Francesco Zorzi told Dezeen. "The ambition was never to recreate Loos's bar, nor Robert and Trix Haussmann's Kronenhalle in Zurich, which was another important reference for the project," he explained. "Rather, we wanted to create a truly classic bar for Milan, with a very specific spatial and architectural character." The studio was informed by Adolf Loos's famous American Bar in Vienna Located just across the road from the city's popular Bar Basso , Bar Bardo is housed within a 55-square-metre single room with an additional bathroom. Almost every element in the listening bar was custom-designed by NM3, known for its modernist-style stainless steel furniture that has already made the young studio a household name in Milan since its founding in 2020. Polished rosewood panels clad the walls and ceilings The walls and ceiling were clad with polished rosewood panels, which add character to the small space while improving its acoustics. A quintessentially NM3 stainless steel bar was placed in the centre of the room, where its gleaming surfaces reflect globular 1950s pendant lights by Italian architect Luigi Caccia Dominioni. The lamps are the only vintage pieces in the bar. NM3 swapped their original chains for longer black ones. Read: Dezeen's favourite wooden furniture and lighting from January The perimeter of the space features built-in red velvet banquette seating, which matches crimson curtains and a series of bright red speakers fitted across the bar to accommodate a stainless steel DJ booth and metal shelving for vinyl records. Bar Bardo was purposefully designed to be a flexible space. Every interior element is movable, with the exception of the bar and the banquettes. "By simply removing the furniture, the cocktail bar can easily be transformed into a club," said Zorzi. "The flexibility of the space is therefore achieved through a simple architectural arrangement rather than complex spatial interventions." The bathroom is characterised by bright red tiles At the back of the space, the striking bathroom was covered with bright red 10-centimetre-by-10-centimetre tiles, from floor to ceiling. Utilitarian stainless steel was once more selected for the toilets, sink and other fixtures, while pared-back sconce lights illuminate the cubicles. NM3's trademark stainless steel was used for the fixtures Bar Bardo marks a softer design direction for NM3. The studio previously conceived a "raw" interior for Milan's Galleria Montegani , as well as a similarly metal-heavy store in the city for fashion brand Miss Sixty. Ahead of Milan design week in April, NM3 was among the studios that spoke to Dezeen about what it's like to be a contemporary designer in Italy's design capital. title: Traditional Thai lanterns inform blue-and-gold Bangkok cafe interior
description: Japanese studio I IN drew on traditional Thai festivals, where thousands of paper lanterns are released into the sky, when creating the interior for the first Blue Bottle Coffee cafe in Bangkok . The interior of the cafe is dominated by the large Blue Lantern installation above the coffee counter. A "Blue Lantern" takes centre stage in this Bangkok cafe "The main idea came from Thailand's traditional lantern festival," I IN co-founder Yohei Terui told Dezeen. "We wanted to capture the feeling of a lantern floating in the sky and bring that into the space in a contemporary way." "This became what we call the Blue Lantern, a large sculptural element extending from the ceiling above the drip station," he continued. I IN wanted to create a dramatic design As it is the brand's first cafe in Bangkok, the studio wanted to design a "bold and dramatic" space that would also nod to local culture. "The lantern idea came from the local culture, and from the beginning, we wanted to make it as large and impactful as possible," Terui said. "We placed it at the location where customers first enter the cafe, so it would immediately catch their attention and become a symbol of the store." Teak was used for the fixtures and furniture The furniture and fixtures in the 178-square-metre cafe were made from teak wood, a material that is often avoided in the West due to concerns about illegal logging , but which is local to Thailand. "Every country has their own approach to natural materials, depending on what is locally available and traditionally used," Terui said. "In Thailand, especially in the north, teak is a very familiar material and commonly used in the interiors and architecture." Read: I IN contrasts concrete architecture with bright colours in Andersson Bell Tokyo store Blue Bottle Coffee cafe Bangkok is drenched in blue hues, with the brand's signature colour used for the lantern and coffee counter. For the rest of the space, I IN chose a pale blue colour to "give guests a sense of brand identity and the feeling of a sky," Terui explained. The cafe also features gold details After visiting the city, the designer also decided to add gold details to the cafe interior. "The idea of bringing gold into the interior actually came from my personal experience of walking around Bangkok," Terui said. "As you walk through the city, you suddenly come across these beautiful, strong gold colours, and I found this contrast very unique," he continued. "It was something that stayed in my memory of Bangkok, and I wanted to bring a little of that feeling into the cafe." I IN also recently designed the concrete Andersson Bell store in Tokyo and clad the Human Made store in Seoul in handcrafted tiles . The photography is by Pichan Sujaritsatit. title: Thin concrete plane defines minimalist villa in Ibiza by Fran Silvestre Arquitectos
description: A thin white-concrete plane folds and steps down a hillside to enclose Bellavista 11, a minimalist home overlooking the sea in Ibiza , designed by Spanish studio Fran Silvestre Arquitectos . Bellavista 11 is the first villa to be completed in The Roca Views development, a cluster of six homes designed by the Valencia-based studio in the town of Roca Lisa on Ibiza's eastern coast. The villas will be united by pared-back, rectilinear forms with thin white walls, designed by Fran Silvestre Arquitectos as a contemporary take on the island's traditional white-walled buildings. Fran Silvestre Arquitectos has completed a minimalist white villa in Ibiza "The project begins with a very simple question, 'Can we build on this hillside by placing a single element on it?'," studio founder Fran Silvestre told Dezeen. "The aim is to create a continuous element that follows the topography and, through its different folds, gradually finds the best conditions offered by the site," he explained. "It is an apparently very simple operation that allows many things to be resolved at once – adapting to the slope, organising the programme, orienting each room towards a different condition of the landscape and extending the architecture to generate shade." The home is framed by a thin concrete plane Bellavista 11 is divided across three low-slung volumes, beginning at the top with a garage and access stair, moving through to a central social volume and ending in a block of five bedrooms. The thin white concrete plane that defines the home is just 15 centimetres thick. As it steps down the site, it creates expansive roof terraces atop the lowest two volumes, folding around to create the interior floor plates and a series of lower terraces. Read: Fran Silvestre Arquitectos creates walkway on top of glazed Hoffman House "We like to think in terms of an evolved tradition, learning from what works in Mediterranean architecture – shade, protection from the sun, clarity of materials – and resolving it through contemporary construction techniques," said Silvestre. Alongside the open-plan living, dining and kitchen space is a swimming pool, while the bedroom block overlooks a seating terrace. Both are accessed via walls of full-height sliding glass doors with slender frames and hidden tracks. It features a terrace with a pool The villa's interiors continue the deliberate simplicity of the exterior, with white walls, pale stone floors and timber carpentry chosen to emphasise the movement of light and shadow across surfaces throughout the day. "White appears naturally because of its relationship with traditional Mediterranean architecture and because of its performance under intense solar radiation," Silvestre explained. "At the same time, it allows light to transform the spaces throughout the day. This is something that particularly interests us, we understand light almost as another material within the project." Minimalist finishes feature throughout the project Silvestre founded his eponymous practice in 2005. The studio previously used a similarly singular geometric gesture for a home in Madrid, which is housed in a cluster of white cylindrical volumes . Its other recent projects include the stepped Villa 95 in Andalusia and the winding Sabater House in Alicante . The photography is by Jesus Orrico . title: OMA dresses faceted French courthouse in coloured glass
description: Dutch studio OMA has completed the Palais de Justice de Lille, a six-sided law court in northern France with a faceted facade lined with coloured glass . Located in Lille, the project was commissioned by the Ministry of Justice to host the city's high and district courts. OMA has completed the Palais de Justice de Lille Palais de Justice de Lille occupies a verdant landscape adjacent to a star-shaped fortification, built in 1667 by the French military engineer Sébastien Le Prestre de Vauban. OMA 's design has a pointy, hexagonal form, with each elevation finished in coloured glass, intended to mimic this fortress. It is lined with coloured glass The Palais de Justice de Lille is arranged in three volumes, accessed via a publicly accessible base. Its first volume is a plinth that holds the major courtrooms, from which a triangular central tower containing minor courtrooms extends. Above, a faceted ring of offices surrounds the tower, which helps draw light into the building. Read: Renzo Piano stacks Toronto courthouse on top of massive atrium According to OMA, each volume has "its own material expression and spatial character, reinforcing clarity and orientation throughout the complex". However, they are unified by light finishes and furnishings, and an ambition to feel welcoming and "free of the intimidation", it added. A series of outdoor spaces complete the project Completing the Palais de Justice de Lille is a series of outdoor spaces, distributed across its three volumes. This includes a public plaza at ground level and a roof garden overlooking the city. A triangular tower contains the minor courtrooms OMA, officially known as Office for Metropolitan Architecture, was founded in 1975 in Rotterdam. It won a competition to design the courthouse in 2018 and was originally due to complete the project in 2023. The studio's other recent projects include an affordable housing development in San Francisco and a pyramidal building in Hangzhou designed as a "three-dimensional village" .
